title: The Rental Documents Checklist: What You Give, and What You Should Get Back
seoTitle: Rental Documents Checklist for Indian Renters
description: Which documents a tenant hands over, what to demand from the owner, what to only ever show, and the paperwork your tenancy should create along the way.
excerpt: Renting in India runs one way: the tenant proves everything, the owner proves nothing. Here is the paperwork on both sides, what to copy, what to refuse, and the single question that separates a real landlord from a man with spare keys.

author.name: The StayOnMap team
author.role: Renters who have handed over too many photocopies

hero.alt: A stack of photocopied ID documents, passport photographs and an electricity bill spread on a table beside a pen

sources.label: India Code — official repository of central legislation, including the Registration Act, 1908
Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs — the Model Tenancy Act, 2021
Ministry of Home Affairs — policing is administered by the states, so check your own state police portal for tenant verification

faq.q: Do I have to give my Aadhaar to a landlord?
faq.a: Aadhaar is the most commonly requested ID, but it is not the only acceptable one. A passport, driving licence, voter ID or PAN is usually fine, and many owners accept whichever you offer first. If you do give an Aadhaar copy, consider the masked version, which hides the first eight digits, and write the purpose and date across the face of the copy so it cannot be reused elsewhere.

faq.q: Is police verification of tenants compulsory in India?
faq.a: It is not a single uniform national rule. Policing is administered at the state level, so the requirement, the form, the online portal and the level of enforcement vary from state to state and often from city to city, and they change over time. In some places it is a housing society rule rather than a police order, which is a different thing entirely. Check your own state police website or ask at the local station rather than relying on a general answer, and keep a copy of whatever is submitted.

faq.q: What proof of ownership should I ask a landlord for?
faq.a: Ask for at least one of: the sale deed or title deed, an allotment and possession letter for a builder flat, the latest property tax receipt, or a recent electricity bill for that flat. All of them should be in the name of the person signing the agreement, and that name should match their photo ID. This is not a legal title search, but three matching documents is a very different position from none. If someone other than the owner is letting the flat, ask for written authority such as a power of attorney.

faq.q: Should I ever hand over original documents?
faq.a: No. Show originals, let them be inspected or photographed if necessary, and keep them. There is no legitimate reason for an owner, a broker or a society office to retain your passport, degree certificate, employment letter or previous agreement. A photocopy serves every purpose an original would in this context, including tenant verification.

faq.q: What should I do if the owner refuses to show any ownership proof?
faq.a: Lower the ask first: skip the sale deed and request the latest electricity bill or property tax receipt, which sit in a drawer rather than a bank locker. Offer to simply view it on their phone instead of taking a copy. Ask why once and listen to the answer, since a genuine explanation comes with specifics while a deflection comes with irritation. If nothing at all is produced, do not pay a deposit, a token or any blocking amount. Walk away.

faq.q: Why keep rent receipts if I pay by bank transfer?
faq.a: Employers and accountants often ask for receipts, and what they require is between you and them. The independent reason to keep them is evidential: a full run of receipts is the owner acknowledging that you paid, in full and on time, which is exactly what you need if a deposit deduction later appears for rent arrears you do not recognise, or if a future landlord asks for a reference. A bank statement does most of this job, but a receipt signed by the owner is stronger.

body:
Ravi counted the photocopies on the auto ride home, because it had started to feel absurd. Aadhaar, front and back. PAN card. Two passport photographs, taken in a hurry at a studio near the bus stand. His offer letter. Three months of salary slips. A bank statement. A copy of his previous rental agreement. And a tenant verification form he'd filled in at the security desk downstairs, in blue ink, because the guard said it had to be blue.

Eleven documents to rent a two-bedroom flat in Whitefield.

The owner showed him nothing. Not one page. Ravi didn't learn the man's full name until it appeared typed on the agreement, and by that point the deposit had already left his account.

That is the shape of renting in India, and it's worth naming out loud. The tenant proves everything. The owner proves nothing. Not because owners are dishonest — most aren't — but because the ritual has always run in one direction and nobody on either side stops to ask why.

This article is about the paper. Not what the agreement *says* — that's a separate piece on [rental agreements](/blog/rental-agreements-in-india) — but which documents actually change hands, who genuinely needs what, what you hand over as a copy versus what you only ever hold up, and the one question that quietly separates a real landlord from a man with a spare set of keys.

## What you will be asked for, and why

Nobody publishes a national list. Every owner, every housing society and every broker has their own idea of a complete file, and the ask ranges from reasonable to faintly ridiculous. But the requests cluster, and after a few flat visits you'll see the same stack every time.

**Photo identity proof.** Aadhaar is the default request. Passport, driving licence, voter ID and PAN are all commonly accepted, and if you'd rather not lead with Aadhaar, offer one of the others first — plenty of owners take a passport or a licence without blinking. PAN is often asked for separately, less as identity and more because it's what goes onto a rent receipt trail.

**Address proof.** Usually your current address, so the owner has somewhere that isn't their own flat associated with your name. A utility bill, a bank statement, or the ID itself if it carries the address.

**Proof that you can pay.** For salaried tenants: an offer or employment letter, an ID card from work, and often two or three months of payslips or bank statements. For self-employed tenants: ITR acknowledgements, GST registration, or bank statements over a longer window. Students get asked for a college ID, an admission or bonafide letter, and almost always a parent or guardian as a guarantor — there's more on that specific situation in the guide to [renting as a student](/blog/renting-as-a-student-in-india).

**Passport photographs.** Two to four, for the agreement and for the society's records. Carry a small stack when you go flat hunting. It's the single most annoying document to be short of at the wrong moment.

**A previous landlord's reference.** Less common, but rising, especially in gated communities. Sometimes it's a phone number, sometimes a signed letter. If your last tenancy ended well, ask for a short reference before you leave — it's much easier to get while you're still a good tenant than six months later.

**A tenant verification form for the local police.** This one deserves its own section.

## Police verification of tenants

You will very likely be handed a form — from the owner, from the society office, or from the security desk — asking for your details, a photograph, ID copies, your previous address and often your employer. This is tenant verification, and it's meant to go to the local police station or, in many cities now, through a state police online portal.

Here's the honest position: **the requirement is not uniform across India.** Policing is administered at the state level, and the rules, the forms, the portals and the degree of enforcement differ from state to state and often from city to city. Some state police forces run a dedicated tenant verification service online. Some cities have issued orders through the local commissionerate. In other places it's a society rule rather than anything issued by the police at all — a real distinction, because a society asking for your papers is not the state asking for them.

So don't take a national rule off the internet, including from this page. Check your own city. Search your state police website for tenant or servant verification, or ask directly at the local station. Ask the owner which route they're using and whether they're filing it or expecting you to.

Two practical things regardless of where you are:

- **Verification is normally the owner's filing, using your details.** If someone tells you it's entirely your job and your cost, ask to see where that's written.
- **Keep a copy of whatever gets submitted, and the acknowledgement if there is one.** It's proof you cooperated, and it's proof of your address on that date, which is occasionally useful for reasons that have nothing to do with the tenancy.

## Now the other direction: what you should ask the owner for

This is the half almost nobody does, and it's the half that protects you from the expensive kind of mistake.

You are about to hand over a large deposit and a year of your life to a person on the basis that they own a flat. Ask them to show you that.

**A photo ID.** The name on it should match the name that will appear on the agreement, and the name on the ownership documents. Sounds obvious. It is routinely not the case.

**Proof of ownership — at least one of these:**

- The **sale deed** or **title deed**, or an **allotment letter** and possession letter for a builder flat.
- The latest **property tax receipt**, in the owner's name, for that address.
- A recent **electricity bill** in the owner's name for that flat and meter.

None of these alone is a legal title search, and this isn't pretending otherwise. But three documents in the same name, matching the ID in front of you and the address you're standing in, is a very different situation from none.

**A society NOC, where the society requires one.** Many housing societies require the owner to obtain a no-objection certificate before letting, and register the tenant with the office. If the society requires it and the owner hasn't got it, that's not your paperwork problem — until the day the security desk won't let your movers in.

**If you're not dealing with the owner, a power of attorney.** Renting through a family member, a caretaker or a "property manager" is completely normal. Renting through one with no written authority from the owner is how a large share of [rental scams](/blog/rental-scams-in-india) start. Ask for the authority in writing, and ask to speak to the owner once, on a call, in front of the flat.

**Bank details, in the owner's name.** If you're transferring rent or a deposit, the account name should match the person signing the agreement. A request to pay into a third party's account is a stop-everything moment.

> You are allowed to ask. That's the whole point of this section. Owners screen tenants as a matter of routine; tenants are somehow expected to take the other side entirely on trust. A polite, specific request — "could you share the tax receipt or an electricity bill in your name, just for my records?" — is normal, and most genuine owners produce it without any fuss at all.

## Copies, showings, and the things you never let out of your hand

The rule is simple and worth holding to even when it feels awkward.

**Never hand over an original.** Not your passport, not your degree certificate, not your employment letter, not your previous agreement. Show it, let it be inspected, let it be photographed if you must — and put it back in your bag. There is no legitimate reason for an owner, a broker or a society office to retain an original document of yours. "We'll return it after the police verification" is not a reason; a photocopy verifies exactly as well.

**Copies are fine, with a marking.** Which brings us to the small habit that costs nothing.

## Marking a photocopy so it can't be reused

Take the photocopy of your ID, and across the face of it — over the printed area, not in the margin, so it can't be cropped out — write in ink:

`For rental agreement, Flat 402 Sai Residency, submitted to Mr S. Kumar, 07-08-2026`

Then sign across it. It takes eleven seconds.

This isn't a legal shield and nobody should sell it as one. What it does is make that specific copy useless for anything else, and make it obvious if it ever turns up somewhere it shouldn't. A clean, unmarked photocopy of your Aadhaar is a portable document. A marked one is evidence of its own purpose.

A few related habits:

- **Count how many copies of your ID are out there.** Over a house hunt you might hand your Aadhaar to four brokers, two owners and a society office without noticing. Some of them will keep the file. Most will keep it badly.
- **Prefer masked Aadhaar** where a full number isn't genuinely needed. The official download option that hides the first eight digits exists precisely for this.
- **Don't send a full ID to a WhatsApp number you got that morning.** Handing paper to a person you've met inside the flat is a different risk entirely. If a listing wants documents before you've seen the property, stop.

## The paperwork your tenancy itself creates

Everything above is entry paperwork. The documents that actually decide how the tenancy ends are the ones generated during it, and this is where most renters go quiet.

**The agreement, both copies signed.** Not a photograph of it on your phone — a physical copy, signed by both parties, with the same date on both. If you don't leave with a signed copy in your hand, chase it that week, not in month nine.

**An inventory and condition report.** A written list of what's in the flat and what state it's in, agreed at handover, with photographs. Wardrobes, geysers, taps, fans, chimney, curtains, the two-year-old stain on the bedroom wall you didn't cause. Both parties sign it. This single document does more to protect a [security deposit](/blog/security-deposits-in-india) than any clause in the agreement, because deposit disputes are almost never about law — they're about whose memory of the wall is correct.

**Meter readings at handover.** Electricity, water, gas, whatever's metered separately. Write the numbers into the inventory, photograph the meters with the readings visible. Then do exactly the same on the day you leave. Inherited arrears are a genuinely common and completely avoidable fight.

**Proof of the deposit payment.** Bank transfer, ideally, with a reference that names it. If any part of it is in cash — try hard for none of it to be — get a signed receipt naming the amount, the date and what it is. Cash with no receipt is a deposit that doesn't exist.

**Rent receipts, every month.**

## Rent receipts: not only for tax season

Most people think of rent receipts as something you assemble in a panic in January because payroll asked for them. They're often needed for exactly that, and your employer or your accountant will tell you what they require — that's their territory, not this article's.

The reason to keep them anyway is different, and simpler.

A twelve-month run of rent receipts is proof that you paid, in full and on time, for twelve months. That matters when a deposit deduction appears for "rent arrears" you don't recognise. It matters when the next owner wants a reference. It matters when the tenancy sours and it becomes your word about payments against theirs.

If rent goes by bank transfer the statement does most of that job — but a receipt is stronger, because it's the owner acknowledging it. Ask monthly. If the owner is slow, send a short message noting the transfer and the amount; a paper trail nobody disputed is worth far more than nothing.

## The checklist: what you give, what you get

Print this, or keep it open on your phone when you go to sign.

| What you hand over | What you should get back |
| --- | --- |
| Photo ID copy (marked with purpose and date) | Owner's photo ID copy, name matching the agreement |
| Address proof copy | Ownership proof: tax receipt, electricity bill, or sale deed / allotment letter |
| Employment or student proof | Society NOC, where the society requires one |
| 2–4 passport photographs | A fully signed copy of the agreement, same date on both |
| Tenant verification form details | The verification acknowledgement, if your city issues one |
| Previous landlord reference, if asked | Signed inventory and condition report, with photographs |
| Deposit and first month's rent | Receipt or transfer record for both, named as deposit and rent |
| — | Meter readings at handover, signed by both |
| — | Rent receipts, monthly |
| — | Owner's contact details and bank account in the owner's own name |

The left column is the one you'll be pushed to complete. The right column is the one that decides how your tenancy ends. Nobody will chase you for it.

## When an owner refuses to show ownership proof

This is the most useful paragraph in the article, so here it is directly.

An owner who will not show any evidence that they can let the flat, after a polite and specific request, has told you something. Take it seriously.

The refusals sound reasonable in the moment. *It's a family property, the papers are with my brother in Delhi.* *The documents are in the bank locker.* *Nobody's ever asked me this before.* *You're asking too many questions for a rented flat.* That last one is the tell — the request is being reframed as rudeness so you'll drop it.

What to do:

1. **Lower the ask.** You don't need the sale deed. Ask for the latest electricity bill, or the property tax receipt. Those are in a drawer, not a locker, and every real owner has one.
2. **Offer a low-friction route.** Ask them to show it on their phone rather than give you a copy. You're looking to see a name and an address, not to keep the document.
3. **Ask why, once, and listen to the shape of the answer.** A genuine explanation — a joint family property, an inheritance still being sorted, an NRI owner with a local relative handling it — comes with specifics and usually with an offer of something else instead. A deflection comes with irritation.
4. **If nothing is produced, don't pay.** No deposit, no token amount, no "blocking" money. Walk. The rental market is not so tight that this is the only flat.

And a hard line worth setting in advance: **never pay a deposit before you have seen the flat, met the person letting it, and seen at least one document connecting them to it.** A token advance to hold a property you've toured, paid to a verified owner, is a normal request. Money sent to hold a flat you've only seen photographs of is not, and it's the single most common way people lose real amounts of money in this market. The [questions to ask before renting](/blog/questions-to-ask-before-renting) are a useful companion to that conversation, and the [hidden costs](/blog/hidden-costs-of-renting-in-india) piece covers what else tends to appear once the paperwork is done.

## Where StayOnMap fits, briefly

We built StayOnMap so that the person you're talking to is the person who owns the flat, rather than an intermediary who collects your documents on the way through. That removes one whole set of copies from the chain, which is a small thing that adds up over a house hunt.

There's an owner verification flow on the platform, and it's worth being precise about what that is: an admin reviews what an owner submits and makes a judgement. It's a signal, not a guarantee, and it doesn't replace a single thing on the right-hand column of that table. Ask for the tax receipt anyway.

Listings state rent, deposit and maintenance upfront, so at least the numbers you're signing against are the numbers you saw.

## The short version

Carry passport photos. Hand over copies, never originals. Write the purpose and the date across every ID copy you give away. Ask your local police or state portal what tenant verification actually requires where you live, rather than trusting a national rule you read somewhere.

And ask the owner for one document — an electricity bill or a tax receipt in their own name. It's a thirty-second request. It's the only part of this whole process that runs in your favour, and almost nobody makes it.

If you're at the start of the search rather than the end, the [house hunting checklist](/blog/house-hunting-checklist-india) covers the ground before the paperwork begins.
